2. Facts necessary for disposal of this Rule are that the petitioners instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration that the ex parte decree and order made in Miscellaneous Case No. 65 of 1966 and the Order of delivery of possession made in Other Execution No. 8 of 1967 of the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania was illegal, fraudulent, void, etc. and for permanent injunction against the defendant and also for a declaration that the defendant was not their co-sharer in the disputed land on the allegations, inter alia, that the land described in schedules 1 and 2 to the plaint originally belonged to one Kamar Ali and on his death the same was devolved upon his son Ibrahim, his two daughters Mazuma and Fatema Khatun. On the death of Mazuma her share devolved upon her brother Ibrahim and her husband Nazu Mia. Ibrahim sold his share to one Dula Miah by a registered kabala dated 21.6.1966, Ext, 1(d). The plaintiffs on the advice of a village tout Abdul Bays handed over some blank cartridge paper with signatures to him for filing a pre-emption case. But as subsequently it transpired that kabala of Dula Mia was followed by deed of reconveyance the plaintiffs did not file the contemplated pre-emption case. Later on reconveyance Ibrahim sold the land to one Altaf Miah by two registered kabalas, Exts. 1 (e) and 1(f), Altaf Miah, in his turn, sold the disputed land to the plaintiffs by registered kabalas dated 24.1.1967, Ext. 1 (b) and 1 (c). While the plaintiffs were in possession of the disputed land the defendant threatened them with dispossession resulting in filing of Other Suit No. 153 of 1967 in the Court of Munsif, 2nd Court, Satkania against the defendant for permanent injunction. It also was alleged that the defendant on the basis of those signed papers fraudulently filed a pre-emption case and obtained an ex parte decree in pre-emption Case No. 65 of 1966. This fact was revealed in the written statement filed by the defendant in Other Suit No. 153 of 1967 which the plaintiffs came to know on 25.10.1967. Hence the plaintiffs filed the present suit on 14.8.72 after withdrawal of Other Suit No. 153 of 1967 on 12.8.72 with the permission from the Court to file a fresh suit. 

 3. The defendant, the predecessors of the present opposite party Nos. 1-5, contested the suit by filing the written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint. His case was that he had purchased the share of Nazu Miah, husband of Mazuma, on 8.1.49 by a registered kabala, Ext. D. and thereby he became co-sharer to the holding and subsequently got the decree in respect of the land sold to Dula Miah by Ibrahim by Ext. 1(d) in the said pre-emption case and also got delivery of possession of the land in dispute. His further case was that purchases of the plaintiffs were also collusive and the plaintiffs had no title and possession in the land in suit. He further pleaded that the suit was not maintainable and was barred by limitation. 

 6. Mr. Mozzamel Hossain submits first, that the lower appellate Court erred in holding that the suit is barred by limitation. He continues to submit that from the pleadings it appears that this is a suit for mere declaration that the decree made in pre-emption case No. 65 of 1966 was void and fraudulent. The learned Advocate read out to me the prayer portion from the plaint to show that the relief sought in the suit is only for declaration and no consequential relief was sought for by way of recovery of possession or confirmation of possession or for setting aside the ex parte decree. He, drawing my attention to this portion, submits that when a suit is a suit for mere declaration without a prayer for consequential relief i.e. to say without a prayer for setting aside the decree or a document the suit is governed by Article 120 and not by Article 95 of the Limitation Act. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred me to the decision in the cases of Province of East Pakistan Vs. A.K.M. Razaul Karim and another, 21 DLR 492 wherein a Division Bench of the then East Pakistan High Court held that a declaratory suit without a prayer for setting aside the order of an official compulsorily retiring from service is governed by Article 120. The learned Advocate further relies upon a decision in the case of FA. Khan Vs. The Government of Pakistan, 16 DLR 405 wherein it has been held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan that starting point for limitation in a suit for declaration that the order of dismissal of the plaintiff was void and inoperative is six years as provided in Article 120 of the Limitation Act. Mr. Hossain, secondly, argues that the Court of app. below committed an error of law in holding that a negative declaration to the effect that the defendant is not a co-sharer is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. In aid of his submission he cited two decisions in the case of Bipin Chandra Roy Vs. Bunchuki Barmani, 37 DLR 49 and in the case Nurul Apsar Vs. Hafizur Rahman Chowdhury and others, 40 DLR 226. 

 7. Mr. M. Fazlul Karim made an attempt to refute the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioners with regard to the question of limitation contending that as the foundation of the plaintiffs suit is based on fraud Article 95 of the Limitation Act is applicable being a specific provision and Article 120 being a residuary article has no role to play in the instant case. In order to appreciate the contentions of the learned Advocates it is necessary to examine both the Articles with reference to the prayers made in this suit. Article 95 refers to a suit for setting aside a decree obtained by fraud. While Article 120 refers to a suit for which no period of limitation is provided elsewhere in the schedule. The present suit is not a suit within the description of Article 95 because it is a suit simpliciter for declaration without a prayer for consequential relief i.e. to say, a decree for setting aside the decree obtained ex parte in the said pre-emption case being Miscellaneous Case No. 65 of 1966. That being the position I do not find any substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the opposite party. It is true, that the foundation of the plaintiffs case is fraud but when it is found that the plaintiffs have only sought for a declaration that a decree made by a court is null and void and have not prayed for setting aside that decree and both the Courts below found that the decree in question was void, the lower appellate Court erred in holding that the suit is barred by limitation on an erroneous view that the provision of Article 95 is attracted to the present case in that the present suit does not fall within the description of a suit covered by Article 95 as no relief by way of setting aside a decree was sought for on the ground of fraud. In order to apply the provisions of Article 95 and Article 120 one is to give due consideration to the frame of the suit. The present suit is quite distinguishable from the one contemplated in Article 95 of the Limitation Act. Thus the first contention of the petitioners is upheld. So far as the second contention regarding negative declaration is concerned it is well covered by two decisions of this Division in one of which I was a party. I myself held in 40 DLR 226 relying b upon 37 DLR 49, which in its turn also relied upon several decisions of Indian jurisdiction. that in a suit wherein a negative declaration is prayed for the suit is not barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for such a prayer. In this case also I have no reason to differ from the principle laid down in Bipin Chandra Roy and in Nurul Apser referred to above, Accordingly, I hold that the lower appellate Court erred in holding that no negative declaration can be made in the present suit.
